claim: IRE1 is an ER membrane-resident kinase/RNase that mediates signal transmission in the most evolutionarily conserved branch of the UPR.
source: Inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1) is an ER membrane-resident kinase/RNase that mediates signal transmission in the most evolutionarily conserved branch of the UPR.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature about IRE1's function and role in the UPR.

claim: The actual oligomeric states of inactive, active, and attenuated mammalian IRE1 complexes remain unknown.
source: Dimerization and/or higher-order oligomerization of IRE1 are thought to be important for its activation mechanism, yet the actual oligomeric states of inactive, active, and attenuated mammalian IRE1 complexes remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study, representing a knowledge gap.

claim: IRE1 exists as a constitutive homodimer at baseline in live cells.
source: In contrast to previous models, our data indicate that IRE1 exists as a constitutive homodimer at baseline and assembles into small oligomers upon ER stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data presented in the manuscript showing that unstressed IRE1 has similar oligomerization to the 2x HaloTag control.

claim: IRE1 assembles into small oligomers upon ER stress.
source: In contrast to previous models, our data indicate that IRE1 exists as a constitutive homodimer at baseline and assembles into small oligomers upon ER stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data showing increased correlated trajectories upon stress treatment.

claim: The formation of inactive dimers and stress-dependent oligomers is fully governed by IRE1's lumenal domain.
source: We demonstrate that the formation of inactive dimers and stress-dependent oligomers is fully governed by IRE1's lumenal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutant analysis data showing that lumenal domain deletions and mutations affect oligomerization.

claim: Phosphorylation of IRE1's kinase domain occurs more slowly than oligomerization.
source: Phosphorylation of IRE1's kinase domain occurs more slowly than oligomerization and is retained after oligomers disassemble back into dimers.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course data comparing oligomerization and phosphorylation kinetics under different stress conditions.

claim: Phosphorylation is retained after oligomers disassemble back into dimers.
source: Phosphorylation of IRE1's kinase domain occurs more slowly than oligomerization and is retained after oligomers disassemble back into dimers.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that oligomerization decreases at 24h while phosphorylation remains.

claim: Assembly of IRE1 dimers into larger oligomers specifically enables trans-autophosphorylation.
source: Our findings suggest that assembly of IRE1 dimers into larger oligomers specifically enables trans-autophosphorylation, which in turn drives IRE1's RNase activity.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the temporal relationship between oligomerization and phosphorylation observed in the data.

claim: Trans-autophosphorylation drives IRE1's RNase activity.
source: Our findings suggest that assembly of IRE1 dimers into larger oligomers specifically enables trans-autophosphorylation, which in turn drives IRE1's RNase activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about IRE1 function and inference from the data.

claim: Upon IRE1 activation by buildup of unfolded proteins in the ER lumen, IRE1 undergoes kinase-mediated trans-autophosphorylation.
source: Upon its activation by the buildup of unfolded proteins in the ER lumen, IRE1 undergoes kinase-mediated trans-autophosphorylation and catalyzes RNase-mediated non-conventional splicing of the XBP1 mRNA (Tirasophon et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2001) (in mammals; HAC1 mRNA in yeast) (Sidrauski and Walter, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IRE1 catalyzes RNase-mediated non-conventional splicing of the XBP1 mRNA in mammals.
source: Upon its activation by the buildup of unfolded proteins in the ER lumen, IRE1 undergoes kinase-mediated trans-autophosphorylation and catalyzes RNase-mediated non-conventional splicing of the XBP1 mRNA (Tirasophon et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2001) (in mammals; HAC1 mRNA in yeast) (Sidrauski and Walter, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IRE1 catalyzes RNase-mediated non-conventional splicing of HAC1 mRNA in yeast.
source: Upon its activation by the buildup of unfolded proteins in the ER lumen, IRE1 undergoes kinase-mediated trans-autophosphorylation and catalyzes RNase-mediated non-conventional splicing of the XBP1 mRNA (Tirasophon et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2001) (in mammals; HAC1 mRNA in yeast) (Sidrauski and Walter, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: IRE1 mediates the decay of multiple mRNA targets via regulated IRE1-decay (RIDD).
source: as well as the decay of multiple mRNA targets via processes termed regulated IRE1-decay (RIDD) (Hollien and Weissman, 2006; Moore and Hollien, 2015; Hollien et al., 2009) and RIDD lacking endomotif (RIDDLE) (Le Thomas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IRE1 mediates the decay of multiple mRNA targets via RIDD lacking endomotif (RIDDLE).
source: as well as the decay of multiple mRNA targets via processes termed regulated IRE1-decay (RIDD) (Hollien and Weissman, 2006; Moore and Hollien, 2015; Hollien et al., 2009) and RIDD lacking endomotif (RIDDLE) (Le Thomas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Both the lumenal and cytosolic domains of yeast IRE1 can individually crystallize as helical filaments.
source: Early work on yeast IRE1 revealed that both the lumenal (Credle et al., 2005) and cytosolic (Korennykh et al., 2009) domains can individually crystallize as helical filaments
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Yeast IRE1 molecules assemble into puncta in the ER membrane upon induction of ER stress.
source: and that IRE1 molecules assemble into puncta in the ER membrane upon induction of ER stress (Kimata et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior microscopy studies.

claim: Fluorescently tagged human IRE1α reversibly assembles into large, topologically complex puncta in a stress-dependent fashion.
source: Similarly, fluorescently tagged human IRE1α ('IRE1' hereafter) was observed to reversibly assemble into large, topologically complex puncta in a stress-dependent fashion (Li et al., 2010; Belyy et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior microscopy studies.

claim: The Hill coefficient for purified yeast IRE1 kinase/RNase domains is approximately 8.
source: The Hill coefficients for purified yeast (Korennykh et al., 2009) and human (Li et al., 2010) IRE1 kinase/RNase domains were measured to be ~8 and ~ 3.4, respectively
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior biochemical studies.

claim: The Hill coefficient for purified human IRE1 kinase/RNase domains is approximately 3.4.
source: The Hill coefficients for purified yeast (Korennykh et al., 2009) and human (Li et al., 2010) IRE1 kinase/RNase domains were measured to be ~8 and ~ 3.4, respectively
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior biochemical studies.

claim: The cooperative formation of oligomers larger than dimers plays an important role in IRE1's enzymatic cycle.
source: The Hill coefficients for purified yeast (Korennykh et al., 2009) and human (Li et al., 2010) IRE1 kinase/RNase domains were measured to be ~8 and ~ 3.4, respectively, indicating that the cooperative formation of oligomers larger than dimers plays an important role in IRE1's enzymatic cycle.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Hill coefficient measurements cited.

claim: The lumenal domain of IRE1 assembles into dimers and larger oligomers in vitro.
source: The lumenal domain, while itself lacking catalytic activity, was also observed to assemble into dimers and larger oligomers in vitro (Gardner and Walter, 2011; Karagöz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: IF1L is the primary dimerization interface of IRE1's lumenal domain.
source: This assembly occurs across two predicted interfaces: IF1L (L for lumenal), generally accepted to be the primary dimerization interface, and IF2L (Figure 1A), which mediates higher order oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: IF2L mediates higher order oligomerization of IRE1's lumenal domain.
source: This assembly occurs across two predicted interfaces: IF1L (L for lumenal), generally accepted to be the primary dimerization interface, and IF2L (Figure 1A), which mediates higher order oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Endogenously tagged IRE1-HaloTag exhibits stress-dependent XBP1 mRNA splicing.
source: UPR activation in IRE1-HaloTag clones was ascertained by the detection of ER stress-dependent XBP1 mRNA splicing (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Endogenously tagged IRE1-HaloTag exhibits stress-dependent IRE1 phosphorylation.
source: UPR activation in IRE1-HaloTag clones was ascertained by the detection of ER stress-dependent XBP1 mRNA splicing (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), IRE1 phosphorylation, production of XBP1s protein, upregulation of the CHOP and ATF4 transcription factors, and cleavage of ATF6 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Endogenously tagged IRE1-HaloTag exhibits stress-dependent production of XBP1s protein.
source: UPR activation in IRE1-HaloTag clones was ascertained by the detection of ER stress-dependent XBP1 mRNA splicing (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), IRE1 phosphorylation, production of XBP1s protein, upregulation of the CHOP and ATF4 transcription factors, and cleavage of ATF6 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Endogenously tagged IRE1-HaloTag exhibits stress-dependent upregulation of CHOP transcription factor.
source: UPR activation in IRE1-HaloTag clones was ascertained by the detection of ER stress-dependent XBP1 mRNA splicing (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), IRE1 phosphorylation, production of XBP1s protein, upregulation of the CHOP and ATF4 transcription factors, and cleavage of ATF6 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Endogenously tagged IRE1-HaloTag exhibits stress-dependent upregulation of ATF4 transcription factor.
source: UPR activation in IRE1-HaloTag clones was ascertained by the detection of ER stress-dependent XBP1 mRNA splicing (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), IRE1 phosphorylation, production of XBP1s protein, upregulation of the CHOP and ATF4 transcription factors, and cleavage of ATF6 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Endogenously tagged IRE1-HaloTag exhibits stress-dependent cleavage of ATF6.
source: UPR activation in IRE1-HaloTag clones was ascertained by the detection of ER stress-dependent XBP1 mRNA splicing (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), IRE1 phosphorylation, production of XBP1s protein, upregulation of the CHOP and ATF4 transcription factors, and cleavage of ATF6 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IRE1-HaloTag cells exhibit RIDD activity as demonstrated by decay of DGAT2, BCAM, and TGOLN2.
source: Furthermore, we found that IRE1-HaloTag cells exhibited RIDD activity, as demonstrated by the decay of the previously described RIDD targets DGAT2, BCAM, and TGOLN2 (Le Thomas et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The endogenous C-terminal HaloTag does not substantially interfere with IRE1's kinase or RNase activity.
source: We concluded that the endogenous C-terminal HaloTag does not substantially interfere with IRE1's kinase or RNase activity and could provide an excellent way to image IRE1 dynamics in live cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the functional assays showing normal UPR activation.

claim: IRE1-HaloTag did not assemble into large clusters upon induction of ER stress at endogenous expression levels.
source: We were surprised to observe that IRE1-HaloTag did not assemble into large clusters upon induction of ER stress (Figure 1E; also see "Detection of Large IRE1 Clusters" in Materials and Methods), in direct contrast to previous work by us and others that relied on ectopic expression of GFP-tagged IRE1 protein (Li et al., 2010; Belyy et al., 2020; Ricci et al., 2019; Ricci et al., 2021; Cohen et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1E and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Overexpression of IRE1-HaloTag by transient transfection results in stress-induced clusters.
source: The lack of clustering was not due to a defect of the IRE1-HaloTag fusion construct, since overexpression of the same IRE1-HaloTag protein by transient transfection resulted in readily observed stress-induced clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The two-color tracking algorithm robustly and reproducibly distinguishes between monomeric and dimeric molecules in the ER membrane.
source: By repeating this analysis on data collected from cells expressing the 1 x and 2 x HaloTag controls in ten independent replicates ( > 10 cells and >1500 trajectories per condition in each replicate), we verified that the algorithm robustly and reproducibly distinguishes between monomeric and dimeric molecules in the ER membrane (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2F across multiple replicates.

claim: The internal and C-terminal HaloTag proteins of the tandem construct have similar labeling efficiencies.
source: To rule out the remote possibility that the 2 x tandem HaloTag protein may be an imperfect control due to differential ligand accessibility of the internal and C-terminal HaloTag proteins, we repeated the analysis with a construct that instead relies on GST dimerization to bring two ER-bound C-terminal HaloTag proteins together (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The measured percentage of co-localized trajectories for this construct was statistically indistinguishable (P = 0.58, two-tailed T-test) from that of the tandem 2 x HaloTag protein
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing data from two different dimeric constructs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 4x HaloTag construct exhibits a substantial increase in the percentage of correlated trajectories compared to the 2x construct.
source: The 4 x HaloTag construct, created by GST-induced dimerization of tandem HaloTag dimers, exhibited a substantial further increase in the percentage of correlated trajectories (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The assay provides excellent sensitivity for oligomers in the monomer to tetramer range.
source: Using a simple combinatoric model relating the observed correlated trajectories to true oligomeric state (See Materials and methods for details), we demonstrated that our assay provides excellent sensitivity for oligomers in the monomer to tetramer range, with sensitivity likely decreasing for oligomers comprised of more than ~10 protomers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fraction of co-localized IRE1 trajectories in non-stressed cells is nearly identical to that of the 2x HaloTag control.
source: In fact, upon quantification, the fraction of co-localized IRE1 trajectories in non-stressed cells appeared nearly identical to that of the 2 x HaloTag control, strongly suggesting that nearly all IRE1 proteins are pre-assembled into dimers at baseline (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Treatment with tunicamycin for 4 hours results in a pronounced increase in the fraction of correlated IRE1 trajectories.
source: Treatment with the glycosylation inhibitor and potent UPR activator tunicamycin (Tm) resulted in a pronounced increase in the fraction of correlated trajectories after 4 hr, indicating that a significant fraction of IRE1 dimers assembled into higher order oligomers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The mean number of molecules per IRE1 cluster increases from approximately 1.8 to approximately 2.5 upon tunicamycin stress.
source: Our model estimates that the mean number of molecules per cluster increases from ~1.8 to ~ 2.5 upon Tm stress (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is an estimate based on the combinatoric model applied to the experimental data.

claim: Extending tunicamycin treatment to 24 hours reverses the shift in correlated trajectories.
source: Extending the treatment to 24 hr reversed the shift in correlated trajectories, suggesting that IRE1 oligomers dissociate back into dimers under prolonged stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: IRE1 oligomers dissociate back into dimers under prolonged stress.
source: Extending the treatment to 24 hr reversed the shift in correlated trajectories, suggesting that IRE1 oligomers dissociate back into dimers under prolonged stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the decrease in correlated trajectories at 24h shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The attenuation of IRE1 oligomerization at 24 hours parallels previously observed attenuation of IRE1 activity upon prolonged, unmitigated ER stress.
source: This finding parallels the previously observed attenuation of IRE1 activity upon prolonged, unmitigated ER stress (Li et al., 2010; Belyy et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2007) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior observations in the literature.

claim: Addition of tunicamycin does not induce an increase in the fraction of correlated trajectories of the 1x and 2x HaloTag controls.
source: Addition of Tm did not induce an increase in the fraction of correlated trajectories of the 1 x and 2 x HaloTag controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the control data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tunicamycin treatment does not affect the efficiency of labeling IRE1-HaloTag with JF dyes.
source: and did not affect the efficiency of labeling IRE1-HaloTag with JF dyes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Diffusion coefficients remain nearly identical among HaloTag controls and IRE1-HaloTag molecules in stressed and unstressed cells.
source: Both approaches showed that diffusion coefficients remain nearly identical among HaloTag controls and IRE1-HaloTag molecules in stressed and unstressed cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the diffusion analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mean apparent diffusion coefficient of unstressed IRE1-HaloTag is 0.18 ± 0.02 µm2 s–1 as measured by the SA method.
source: the SA method resulted in a far tighter distribution than the MSD method and yielded a mean apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.18 ± 0.02 µm2 s–1 for unstressed IRE1-HaloTag
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the data using the SA method.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of 0.18 µm2 s–1 for IRE1-HaloTag is close to the value of 0.24 µm2 s–1 obtained previously for IRE1-mNeonGreen by FRAP.
source: which is remarkably close to the value of 0.24 ± 0.02 µm2 s–1 that we obtained previously for IRE1-mNeonGreen by FRAP (Belyy et al., 2020).
evidence: This compares the current measurement to a prior measurement from the same lab.

claim: Thapsigargin induces IRE1 phosphorylation much more rapidly and strongly than tunicamycin.
source: Intriguingly, thapsigargin (Tg), which disrupts ER calcium homeostasis by blocking sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ pumps (Lu et al., 2014), induced IRE1 phosphorylation much more rapidly and strongly than Tm, despite leading to similar overall levels of XBP1s production (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Thapsigargin and tunicamycin lead to similar overall levels of XBP1s production.
source: Intriguingly, thapsigargin (Tg), which disrupts ER calcium homeostasis by blocking sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ pumps (Lu et al., 2014), induced IRE1 phosphorylation much more rapidly and strongly than Tm, despite leading to similar overall levels of XBP1s production (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with dithiothreitol induces IRE1 oligomerization to the same extent as tunicamycin.
source: Treatment with dithiothreitol (DTT), which causes protein misfolding by reducing disulfide bonds, induced IRE1 oligomerization to the same extent as Tm (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Treatment with 100 nM thapsigargin for 2 or 4 hours does not induce a detectable change in IRE1 oligomeric state.
source: However, to our surprise, treatment with a high concentration (100 nM) of Tg did not induce a detectable change in oligomeric state either 2 or 4 hr after treatment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Imaging cells 10 minutes after addition of 100 nM thapsigargin reveals a robust increase in IRE1 oligomerization.
source: Indeed, imaging cells only 10 min after the addition of 100 nM Tg revealed a robust increase in IRE1 oligomerization, as indicated by an increase in the fraction of correlated trajectories (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A lower concentration of 1 nM thapsigargin leads to IRE1 oligomerization at 2 and 4 hour time-points.
source: Furthermore, a lower concentration of 1 nM Tg led to IRE1 oligomerization at the longer 2- and 4 hr time-points.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: When 100 nM thapsigargin is combined with saturating tunicamycin, there is no detectable IRE1 oligomerization 4 hours after treatment.
source: Meanwhile, when 100 nM Tg was combined with saturating Tm, there was no detectable IRE1 oligomerization 4 hr after treatment, demonstrating that the repressive effect of extended Tg treatment overrides the pro-oligomerization effect of Tm.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: All commonly used ER stressors induce IRE1 oligomerization, albeit on different temporal scales.
source: Taken together, our results show that IRE1 phosphorylation lags behind oligomerization and that all commonly used ER stressors induce IRE1 oligomerization, albeit on different temporal scales.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data comparing different stressors shown in Figure 4.

claim: IRE1 remains dimeric in unstressed cells even at decreased expression levels.
source: IRE1 remained dimeric in unstressed cells even at this decreased expression level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data from the low-expressing clone shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The extent of stress-induced oligomerization is markedly reduced in the low-expressing IRE1-HaloTag clone.
source: Meanwhile, the extent of stress-induced oligomerization was markedly reduced, mirroring the decrease in production of XBP1s protein by these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing data from high and low expressing clones in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The K121Y mutation disrupts the IF1L interface of the IRE1 lumenal domain.
source: The first revealing pair of functional mutants comprised K121Y, which disrupts the IF1L interface of the IRE1 lumenal domain (Li et al., 2010)
evidence: This is based on prior characterization of this mutant cited in the text.

claim: The WLLI359-362-GSGS mutation disrupts the lumenal domain's oligomerization interface IF2L.
source: and WLLI359-362-GSGS, which disrupts the lumenal domain's oligomerization interface IF2L (Karagöz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on prior characterization of this mutant cited in the text.

claim: The K121Y mutant remains similar to the 1x HaloTag control in oligomeric state both with and without ER stress.
source: The oligomeric state of K121Y remained similar to that of the 1 x HaloTag control, both with and without induction of ER stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The WLLI359-362-GSGS mutant retains the same oligomeric state as unstressed WT IRE1 both with and without ER stress.
source: In contrast, WLLI359-362-GSGS retained the same oligomeric state as unstressed WT IRE1 both with (p = 0.74) and without (p = 0.18) ER stress (two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mutant data shown in Figure 5 with statistical analysis.

claim: Both lumenal domain mutants fail to change their oligomeric states in response to ER stress.
source: Thus, both lumenal domain mutants fail to change their oligomeric states in response to ER stress, with K121Y remaining mostly monomeric and WLLI359-362-GSGS remaining mostly dimeric.
evidence: This is a summary of the mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The K599A mutation abrogates IRE1's kinase activity.
source: K599A, a mutation that abrogates IRE1's kinase activity (Tirasophon et al., 1998)
evidence: This is based on prior characterization of this mutant cited in the text.

claim: The K599A mutant closely resembles the phenotype of WT IRE1 in oligomerization.
source: K599A, a mutation that abrogates IRE1's kinase activity (Tirasophon et al., 1998), closely resembled the phenotype of WT IRE1, with only a slightly reduced difference in oligomerization between the non-stress and stress conditions (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The delta-LD construct (deletion of lumenal domain) remains purely monomeric regardless of ER stress.
source: Remarkably, the delta-LD construct remained purely monomeric regardless of ER stress (p = 0.92 and p = 0.64 for unstressed and stressed cells, respectively, when compared to the 1 x HaloTag control; two-tailed t-test)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mutant data shown in Figure 5 with statistical analysis.

claim: The delta-KR construct (deletion of kinase/RNase domain) recapitulates the stress-dependent transition from dimers to higher order oligomers.
source: while the delta-KR construct recapitulated the stress-dependent transition from dimers to higher order oligomers (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The lumenal domain serves as the central governor of IRE1 oligomerization.
source: Taken together, the mutant data confirm the previously proposed role of the lumenal domain as the central governor of IRE1 oligomerization, consistent with its role as the ER stress sensor domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both constitutive dimerization and the dimer-to-oligomer transition are entirely controlled by the lumenal domain of IRE1.
source: Both constitutive dimerization and the dimer-to-oligomer transition appear to be entirely controlled by the lumenal domain of IRE1, with the kinase and RNase domains acting downstream.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The kinase and RNase domains act downstream of the lumenal domain in IRE1 oligomerization.
source: Both constitutive dimerization and the dimer-to-oligomer transition appear to be entirely controlled by the lumenal domain of IRE1, with the kinase and RNase domains acting downstream.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: IRE1 forms constitutive inactive dimers in the absence of externally induced ER stress in U-2 OS cells.
source: Surprisingly, IRE1 forms constitutive inactive dimers in the absence of externally induced ER stress in U-2 OS cells, thus challenging the widely held notion (Amin-Wetzel et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2000; Pincus et al., 2010) that the monomer-to-dimer equilibrium constitutes the primary regulatory step in IRE1 activation.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study based on the single-molecule tracking data.

claim: The lumenal domain alone is sufficient for the formation of both resting-state dimers and stress-induced oligomers when tethered to the ER membrane.
source: Indeed, the lumenal domain alone is sufficient for the formation of both resting-state dimers and stress-induced oligomers when tethered to the ER membrane, while the kinase/RNase domain alone remains strictly monomeric.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the delta-KR and delta-LD mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The kinase/RNase domain alone remains strictly monomeric.
source: Indeed, the lumenal domain alone is sufficient for the formation of both resting-state dimers and stress-induced oligomers when tethered to the ER membrane, while the kinase/RNase domain alone remains strictly monomeric.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the delta-LD mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The kinase/RNase domains can adopt two distinct dimeric conformations: back-to-back and face-to-face orientations.
source: The kinase/RNase domains can adopt two distinct dimeric conformations, known as the back-to-back and face-to-face orientations (Korennykh and Walter, 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior structural and biochemical studies cited in the text.

claim: The back-to-back orientation is thought to represent the RNase-active form of IRE1.
source: The back-to-back orientation is thought to represent the RNase-active form of the protein, but is incapable of trans-autophosphorylation since both kinase active sites face outwards.
evidence: This is based on prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The back-to-back orientation is incapable of trans-autophosphorylation since both kinase active sites face outwards.
source: The back-to-back orientation is thought to represent the RNase-active form of the protein, but is incapable of trans-autophosphorylation since both kinase active sites face outwards.
evidence: This is based on structural considerations from prior studies.

claim: The face-to-face arrangement is suited for trans-autophosphorylation but is not expected to have RNase activity.
source: Meanwhile, the face-to-face arrangement is perfectly suited for trans-autophosphorylation but is not expected to have RNase activity (Korennykh and Walter, 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior structural and biochemical studies cited in the text.

claim: Naive IRE1 is either partially or fully pre-assembled into back-to-back dimers, which remain inactive due to their lack of phosphorylation.
source: Our data favor an alternative model (Figure 6), wherein naive IRE1 is either partially or fully pre-assembled into back-to-back dimers, which remain inactive due to their lack of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data from this study, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: In response to ER stress, the lumenal domains drive the assembly of higher order oligomers such as tetramers.
source: In response to ER stress, the lumenal domains drive the assembly of higher order oligomers such as tetramers (that is, dimers of dimers).
evidence: This is part of the model proposed based on the data from this study.

claim: The formation of tetramers permits inter-dimer face-to-face interactions of kinase-RNase domains, enabling phosphorylation.
source: Since the back-to-back interfaces are already engaged, the formation of tetramers permits inter-dimer face-to-face interactions of kinase-RNase domains, thus enabling the phosphorylation reaction that in turn activates the RNase domains of the back-to-back dimers.
evidence: This is part of the model proposed based on the data from this study.

claim: The unimpeded ability of K599A to form dimers and oligomers supports that phosphorylation takes place at the level of higher order oligomers rather than dimers.
source: The unimpeded ability of K599A to form dimers and oligomers further supports the notion that phosphorylation takes place at the level of higher order oligomers rather than dimers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the K599A mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The larger oligomers may represent a phosphorylation-competent transient state en route to generating fully active phosphorylated dimers.
source: Our results raise the question of whether the larger oligomers represent the maximally active form of IRE1 or are instead a phosphorylation-competent transient state en route to the generation of fully active phosphorylated dimers with and perhaps outside of oligomers.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the oligomers based on the data.

claim: Fast assembly and disassembly of high-order oligomers in response to saturating thapsigargin, coupled with rapid hyper-phosphorylation, suggest that phosphorylated IRE1 may not need to remain oligomeric for its RNase to remain active.
source: Our data showing the fast assembly and disassembly of high-order oligomers in response to saturating Tg, coupled with rapid hyper-phosphorylation, suggest that phosphorylated IRE1 may not need to remain oligomeric for its RNase to remain active.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the thapsigargin time-course data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Extensive phosphorylation on IRE1's kinase domain may serve as a negative feedback mechanism.
source: In fact, extensive phosphorylation either on the activation loop or elsewhere on IRE1's kinase domain may serve as a negative feedback mechanism, as previously proposed for yeast IRE1 (Rubio et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on prior work on yeast IRE1 cited in the text.

claim: Electrostatic repulsion across the face-to-face interface of two hyperphosphorylated dimers within an oligomer may break them apart into active back-to-back dimers.
source: A simple potential model for such negative feedback is that electrostatic repulsion across the face-to-face interface of two hyperphosphorylated dimers within an oligomer may break them apart into active back-to-back dimers and render the phosphate groups more accessible to the action of regulatory phosphatases (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the negative feedback mechanism.

claim: A small fraction of IRE1 monomers may remain in equilibrium with a largely dimeric resting population.
source: First, the single-particle tracking approach does not rule out the existence of monomeric IRE1; it is entirely plausible that a small fraction of monomers remain in equilibrium with a largely dimeric resting population.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the method and allows for the possibility of some monomers.

claim: Transient monomerization of the IF1L interface may play an important role in the regulated attenuation of IRE1 signaling in response to prolonged stress.
source: Transient monomerization of the IF1L interface, for example through the action of ER-lumenal chaperones (Amin-Wetzel et al., 2017), may play an important role in the regulated attenuation of IRE1 signaling in response to prolonged stress as previously suggested (Pincus et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism based on prior literature.

claim: Mammalian IRE1 has the capacity to assemble into clusters larger than tetramers, and such clustering may largely be a function of protein expression level.
source: Conversely, we do not claim that mammalian IRE1 lacks the capacity to assemble into clusters larger than tetramers; as with any oligomerization-prone protein, such clustering may largely be a function of protein expression level.
evidence: This acknowledges that larger clusters can form under certain conditions.

claim: The substantially lower expression levels achieved in this study are likely the reason that endogenously tagged IRE1 did not assemble into large clusters.
source: The substantially lower expression levels achieved in this study are likely the reason that we did not observe endogenously tagged IRE1 assembling into large clusters.
evidence: This is an inference about why clusters were not observed at endogenous expression levels.

claim: IRE1 clustering is not an artifact of fluorescent protein fusions.
source: Conversely, we can rule out the possibility that IRE1 clustering is an artifact of fluorescent protein fusions. In a parallel study by Gómez-Puerta et al., the authors expressed IRE1-GFP in HeLa cells at near-endogenous levels and demonstrated that it remains fully active despite not forming microscopically detectable clusters (Gómez-Puerta et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a parallel study.

claim: Nearly one half of cells overexpressing IRE1-mNeonGreen did not form clusters over the time course of stress, despite fully splicing XBP1 mRNA.
source: Furthermore, in an earlier study from our own lab, we found that nearly one half of cells overexpressing an IRE1-mNeonGreen reporter did not form clusters over the time course of stress, despite fully splicing XBP1 mRNA (Belyy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the same lab.

claim: Large IRE1 clusters do not artificially result from overexpression.
source: We also do not contend that large IRE1 clusters artificially result from overexpression: IRE1 levels were found to be highly variable across a panel of cancer cell lines (Harnoss et al., 2019; Harnoss et al., 2020) and it is reasonable to suspect that large clusters of endogenous IRE1 do form in cell lines with elevated amounts of IRE1 protein.
evidence: This is based on prior observations of variable IRE1 expression in cancer cell lines.

claim: IRE1 has the propensity to preassemble into inactive dimers in the absence of stress induction.
source: Rather than entirely ruling out the existence of IRE1 monomers or large oligomers, the present study demonstrates that IRE1 has the propensity to preassemble into inactive dimers in the absence of stress induction and that oligomerization past the tetrameric state is not strictly required for its RNase activation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study based on the data.

claim: Oligomerization past the tetrameric state is not strictly required for IRE1's RNase activation.
source: Rather than entirely ruling out the existence of IRE1 monomers or large oligomers, the present study demonstrates that IRE1 has the propensity to preassemble into inactive dimers in the absence of stress induction and that oligomerization past the tetrameric state is not strictly required for its RNase activation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study based on the data.

claim: In solution reactions, kinase/RNase dimers are capable of performing stem-loop endomotif-specific mRNA cleavage.
source: In solution reactions, kinase/RNase dimers are capable of performing stem-loop endomotif-specific mRNA cleavage, while phosphorylated oligomers perform this function more efficiently than dimers and acquire a more promiscuous RNase activity termed RIDDLE (Le Thomas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited in the text.

claim: Phosphorylated oligomers perform stem-loop endomotif-specific mRNA cleavage more efficiently than dimers and acquire RIDDLE activity.
source: In solution reactions, kinase/RNase dimers are capable of performing stem-loop endomotif-specific mRNA cleavage, while phosphorylated oligomers perform this function more efficiently than dimers and acquire a more promiscuous RNase activity termed RIDDLE (Le Thomas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited in the text.

claim: In a cellular context, non-phosphorylated full-length IRE1 dimers are more restricted, and even endomotif-directed RNase activity requires IRE1 oligomerization and phosphorylation.
source: The present data suggest that in a cellular context, non-phosphorylated full-length IRE1 dimers are more restricted, perhaps by orientation, while even endomotif-directed RNase activity requires IRE1 oligomerization and phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the current cellular data to prior in vitro studies.

claim: The restriction of non-phosphorylated IRE1 dimers may be steric, due to limited ability to adopt a conformation conducive to RNA cleavage.
source: This restriction may be simply steric, due to the limited ability of the unphosphorylated membrane-tethered kinase/RNase dimers to adopt a conformation conducive to RNA cleavage
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of restriction.

claim: The restriction of non-phosphorylated IRE1 dimers may arise from IRE1's association with the ribosome and/or the Sec61 translocon.
source: or it may arise from IRE1's association with supplementary molecular players such as the ribosome (Acosta-Alvear et al., 2018) and/or the Sec61 translocon (Sundaram et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms based on prior literature.

claim: Lipid saturation activates IRE1 independently of its lumenal domain.
source: Additionally, it remains to be determined how other signals—such as lipid saturation, which has been found to activate IRE1 independently of its lumenal domain (Volmer et al., 2013)—impact IRE1's oligomerization and phosphorylation states.
evidence: This is based on prior studies cited in the text.

claim: Changes in the ER membrane's lipid composition likely drive IRE1 molecules into phosphorylation-competent small oligomers via key features of IRE1's transmembrane helix.
source: Based on prior work in the field, it is likely that changes in the ER membrane's lipid composition directly drive IRE1 molecules into phosphorylation-competent small oligomers via key features of IRE1's transmembrane helix (Kono et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work cited in the text.
